preferences.session_flow: Complete the current session fully and in order before diverting to side topics.

observed_successes: Selected a Go map/set for membership-by-ID and explained that the ID is the lookup key.
Recognized that last-N event queries need ordered occurrences, including duplicates; proposed a queue/bounded slice for A, B, A and correctly identified B, A as the last two.
Worked through bounded-slice versus circular-buffer tradeoffs and understood that a ring buffer avoids O(k) shifting by overwriting at a wrapped index.
Explained that a linear scan is acceptable when the collection is tiny, lookups are infrequent, or all items must be scanned anyway.
Extracted operations from a priority-task prompt as insert plus get-highest-priority and selected a heap.
Understood the distinction between map+doubly-linked-list for known-position moves such as move-to-front and heap+ID-index for priority-driven reordering.
Understood that arbitrary heap-item lookup is supplied by the auxiliary map, while the heap provides O(log n) order repair along a parent-child path.
Understood the binary-heap array representation and parent/child index relationships conceptually.
Recognized that deleting from an indexed slice invalidates stored positions, and proposed a map-to-linked-list-node alternative plus the swap-with-last optimization when order does not matter.
Explained why slice append is amortized O(1): most appends are cheap, while occasional resize-and-copy costs are spread across many appends.
Correctly identified that Go len(s) counts bytes rather than Unicode code points and clarified the distinction between bytes, code points/runes, and user-perceived characters.
Correctly explained that a min-heap efficiently returns the task with the smallest deadline but does not efficiently find an arbitrary task by ID without an auxiliary index.
Correctly computed that 1,000 users with up to 100 timestamps each can retain up to 100,000 timestamps, recognizing that per-user capacity is not the total memory bound.
Correctly reasoned that total retained timestamps in a map of per-user queues scale as users times per-user capacity.
Proposed a valid alternative undo design where a map points from document ID to the latest version while the version history stores the actual document contents.

Completed the Round 12 teach-back: described saving a new document version by pushing the old version to history and updating current state, undo by restoring history, and identified atomicity as the key consistency obligation.
Completed the one-minute representation summary, including identity lookup, ordering, stacks, queues/heaps, and map plus doubly-linked-list tradeoffs.
Designed an in-memory event registry using a map for O(1) average ID lookup plus an ordered structure for arrival order, with synchronized eviction from both structures at capacity.
Explained remove-by-ID using a map to locate a doubly-linked-list node, O(1) unlinking, and deletion from the map.
Reasoned that if arbitrary removal is extremely rare, a simpler map plus slice/ring-buffer design can be preferable despite O(n) rare removals.
Understood recent(n) as walking from the newest end and reversing the collected result when oldest-to-newest output is required.
Started concurrency design with a single mutex and then understood sync.RWMutex: readers share RLock while writers take exclusive Lock.
prompted_successes: After explanation, understood why a fixed-capacity circular buffer may still need logical-size tracking depending on slice initialization.
After clarification, distinguished the linked-list O(1) node lookup/removal from the O(n) search for a new sorted-by-priority insertion position.
After explanation, understood Go's comma-ok map lookup and that missing keys return the zero value with ok=false.
After explanation, understood that passing a slice by value copies the slice header while sharing the backing array, and that cloning/copying elements creates isolation.
After the retained-memory issue was explained, proposed a fixed-size circular buffer with wraparound head movement as a bounded-queue solution.
After correction, understood that the undo stack represents history while the map represents current document state, and that undo must keep those two representations consistent.
After discussion, distinguished the conventional current-state map plus command stack design from a map-to-version-history design and understood the consistency requirements of each.
After prompting, recognized that an array-backed queue requires O(n) middle removal and switched to map plus doubly-linked-list for O(1) known-node removal.
After clarification, distinguished get(id) from dequeue/evict-oldest operations.
After prompting, understood that recent(n) needs no heap, stack, or binary search because the existing ordered list already encodes arrival order.
After explanation, understood why read operations still require RLock with sync.RWMutex: readers do not need protection from each other, but they must be synchronized against writers.
